title: Stacks and queues

story.title: Undo in a text editor and the office print queue
story.summary: You build two features: an editor whose Ctrl+Z takes back edits, and a print queue that serves jobs. Each needs its own order of removal, and both must stay fast when the history or the queue grows long.

uses.title: Undo history in editors
uses.body: An editor records each change on a history, and Ctrl+Z takes the latest change back first. Many editors keep this history as a stack.

uses.title: The call stack of a program
uses.body: When a function is called, the runtime pushes a frame for it, and when the function returns, the frame is popped. The call that started last always finishes first.

uses.title: Print spoolers
uses.body: A print spooler lines up documents and, by default, sends them to the printer in the order they arrived.

uses.title: Keyboard input buffers
uses.body: The operating system keeps your keystrokes in a queue, so an app that is busy for a moment still reads them in the order you typed them.

whenNot: A stack or a queue only gives you its ends: the top of a stack, or the front and the back of a queue. If you need to read or change the fifth edit in the middle, an array fits better, because only an array reads by position in O(1), while a linked list has to walk to it. If the next item to serve is neither the newest nor the oldest, such as the most urgent print job, you need a priority queue, which comes later in the Course.

overview.title: Two ways to hold items in order
overview.caption: A [[stack]] and a [[queue]] both hold items in order, and they differ in which item leaves first. A stack gives back the newest item first, called last in, first out. A queue gives back the oldest item first, called first in, first out. The drawing shows an example of each: an undo history and a print queue.

the-problem.title: Undo has to find the right edit
the-problem.caption: You build undo for an editor, where a writer types a line, bolds a word and pastes a paragraph. The editor keeps these edits in the order they happened. Every Ctrl+Z has to take back the right edit, even when the history holds thousands of them, and you must find it at once without searching. The printer in the same office will need a different rule, which you meet later.
the-problem.keyIdea: Some jobs need the newest item first, and others need the oldest first.

push-edits.title: Each edit goes on top
push-edits.caption: You start with an empty undo stack, where you touch only one end, called the top. You type a line, bold a word, then paste. Each edit goes onto the stack with [[push]], which places it on top of the items already there. Type goes in first, then Bold, then Paste.
push-edits.keyIdea: A stack gives back its newest item first: last in, first out.

undo-pops.title: Undo takes the top
undo-pops.caption: You press Ctrl+Z. The editor removes the top edit from the stack with [[pop]] and takes that edit back. Pop touches only the top, so the other edits stay exactly where they were.

new-edit-after-undo.title: A new edit goes on top again
new-edit-after-undo.caption: You delete a line, and the editor pushes Delete onto the stack. The next Ctrl+Z pops Delete, because the newest edit is always the one on top. Type and Bold wait underneath.

constant-time.title: Push and pop never search
constant-time.caption: You apply Italic, and the editor pushes it on top. Push and pop touch only the top, so they take the same work with 2 edits or 100,000. Nothing is searched, so pop costs O(1), and push costs O(1) amortised for an array-backed stack, because the array occasionally has to grow.
constant-time.keyIdea: Pop costs O(1), and push costs O(1) amortised for an array-backed stack.

a-queue.title: The printer follows the opposite rule
a-queue.caption: Now the office printer. Jobs must come out in the order they were sent, so the job that has waited longest goes first. A queue works this way: jobs join at the back and leave from the front. The print queue starts empty.
a-queue.keyIdea: A queue gives back its oldest item first: first in, first out.

enqueue-jobs.title: Jobs join at the back
enqueue-jobs.caption: You send three jobs one after another: first Report, then Invoice, then Ticket. [[enqueue]] adds a job at the back of the queue. The queue keeps the jobs in arrival order.

dequeue-print.title: The printer takes the front job
dequeue-print.caption: The printer is free and takes its next job with [[dequeue]], which removes the item at the front. Report leaves the queue and the printer starts on it. The jobs behind it keep waiting.

late-job.title: A late job waits its turn
late-job.caption: You add a late job, Poster, at the back of the queue. The printer then takes two jobs, one after the other. Only Poster is left, because every job ahead of it has gone.

stack-vs-queue.title: Same items, different order out
stack-vs-queue.caption: Here a stack and a queue both hold items in the order they arrived, from left to right. The stack gives back Paste, its newest item, and the queue gives back Poster, its oldest. The operations make a structure a stack or a queue, not the items inside it.
stack-vs-queue.keyIdea: A stack returns the newest item and a queue returns the oldest.

bracket-preview.title: Next up: check the brackets
bracket-preview.caption: In Practice you check that every (, [ and { in a line of code is closed in the right order. A stack suits that job, because the bracket opened last has to be closed first. The open brackets shown are ( and [, so [ has to close before ( can.

where-you-meet-it.title: Where you will meet them
where-you-meet-it.caption: Here is where you meet stacks and queues outside this office. Each hands back items in an order that never changes. The note under them says when to pick something else.

which-edit-is-undone.prompt: The undo stack holds Type, Bold and Paste, pushed in that order. You press Ctrl+Z. Select the edit that is undone.
which-edit-is-undone.explanation: Paste is undone, because it sits on top and a stack gives back only its top. Bold lies directly below Paste, so it can come up only after Paste is gone. Type is at the bottom, so it is undone last.

undo-after-a-new-edit.prompt: You undid Paste, so the stack holds Type and Bold. Now you delete a line, which is a new edit, and press Ctrl+Z. Which edit is undone?

options.delete-on-top: Delete, because the newest edit sits on top
options.paste-comes-back: Paste, because the editor returns to the edit it undid last
options.bold-under-new: Bold, because a new edit joins at the bottom of the stack
options.oldest-first: Type, because Ctrl+Z always takes back the oldest edit

undo-after-a-new-edit.explanation: Delete is undone, because push puts every new edit on top and pop takes the top. Paste is gone from the stack once it is undone, so nothing brings it back first. A new edit never joins at the bottom: that is how a queue grows, not a stack. A stack never reaches for its oldest item first, because Type lies at the bottom.

cost-of-push-on-a-long-history.prompt: The undo history grows from 2 edits to 100,000. Roughly how much work does one push or one pop need?

options.same-small-work: The same small amount as before, because both touch only the top: pop is O(1) and push is O(1) amortised for an array-backed stack
options.shift-all: More work with every edit, because a push or a pop shifts all the edits: O(n)
options.walk-to-spot: More work with every edit, because a push or a pop first walks down to find its place: O(n)
options.halving: About log n steps, because a push or a pop finds its place by halving the history

cost-of-push-on-a-long-history.explanation: Pop costs O(1) and push costs O(1) amortised for an array-backed stack, because both touch only the top and the other edits do not matter. Nothing shifts, because the new edit goes on top of the pile instead of into a numbered position. Nothing is searched either, because the place is always the top. Halving applies to searching a sorted array, and a stack never searches.

which-job-prints-first.prompt: The print queue holds Report, Invoice and Ticket, sent in that order. The printer is free. Select the job it takes.
which-job-prints-first.explanation: The printer takes Report, because it is at the front and has waited longest. A queue serves jobs in arrival order. Ticket, the newest job, is at the back and goes last. Invoice sits right behind Report and goes second.

print-order-with-a-late-job.prompt: Report has printed, and Invoice and Ticket are still waiting. Then a new job, Poster, arrives. In what order do the three remaining jobs print?

options.back-of-queue: Invoice, Ticket, Poster, because a new job joins at the back and waits its turn
options.front-of-queue: Poster, Invoice, Ticket, because a new job joins at the front
options.newest-first: Poster, Ticket, Invoice, because the printer takes the newest job first, as undo does
options.short-jobs-first: Invoice, Poster, Ticket, because a queue lets a short job go ahead

print-order-with-a-late-job.explanation: The order is Invoice, Ticket, Poster, because enqueue adds Poster at the back and dequeue takes from the front. A new job does not join the front, and a queue never lets a job skip ahead. Taking the newest job first is the rule of a stack, not of a queue. A queue knows nothing about job length, so it never reorders by it.

structure-for-redo.prompt: The editor gets a Redo button. Undone edits come back, and the edit undone most recently comes back first. Which structure should hold the undone edits?

options.stack-for-redo: A stack, because the edit added last has to leave first
options.queue-for-redo: A queue, because undone edits should come back in the order they were undone
options.either-for-redo: Either one, because both give items back from an end

structure-for-redo.explanation: A stack fits, because the most recently undone edit is the one added last and has to leave first. A queue would return the edit undone first, which is the opposite of what Redo needs. Both structures give items back from an end, but they pick different ends, so the choice decides which edit comes back.

stack.gloss: A pile of items where you add and remove only at the top, so the newest item leaves first.

push.gloss: Adding an item on top of a stack.

pop.gloss: Removing and returning the top item of a stack.

queue.gloss: A line of items where you add at the back and remove at the front, so the oldest item leaves first.

enqueue.gloss: Adding an item at the back of a queue.

dequeue.gloss: Removing and returning the item at the front of a queue.

exercise.title: Check the brackets in a line
exercise.task: The editor flags a line of code whose brackets are wrong. Write isBalanced, which takes a line of code and returns true when every (, [ and { is closed by the matching ), ] or } in the right order. Ignore every other character, and let a [[stack]] help you so one pass over the line is enough.
hints: Look at the order in which brackets must close: the one opened last has to close first. Which structure gives back its newest item first?
Only opening brackets need remembering, and every other character can be skipped. Think about what a closing bracket should be compared with.
A closing bracket with nothing open has nothing to match. When the line ends, check what is left over: an opening bracket that never closed makes the line unbalanced.
